title: Two Meta-Analyses Exploring the Relationship Between Teacher Clarity and Student Learning https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03634523.2015.1041998
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page covers a pair of meta-analyses by Titsworth, Mazer, Goodboy, Bolkan, and Myers that quantify the relationship between teacher clarity and student learning. The first, spanning 144 studies, finds teacher clarity accounts for roughly 13 percent of the variance in student learning, with a stronger relationship to affective learning (attitudes and engagement) than to cognitive learning (understanding and recall). The second, drawing on 46 studies, confirms a moderate effect on both types of learning but shows that study design significantly moderates the size of the effect on affective outcomes. Both analyses report substantial heterogeneity across studies, which the authors attribute to inconsistent operationalizations of 'clarity' and call for more low-inference, behaviorally specific measurement going forward. Barton highlights the practical guidance that follows: teachers should anchor clarity in specific, observable behaviors -- previewing lesson structure, giving concise explanations, using relevant examples, checking understanding -- rather than relying on vague self-impressions of being 'clear'. The authors also flag a caution that clarity can be overdone, tipping into redundancy and student frustration if taken too far.
points: Across 144 studies, teacher clarity explains around 13% of the variance in student learning, with a stronger link to affective than cognitive learning.
A second 46-study meta-analysis confirms a moderate clarity effect on both learning types but shows study design substantially moderates the affective-learning result.
Clarity should be measured through specific, low-inference behaviors -- previewing structure, concise explanations, relevant examples, checking understanding -- not vague global impressions.
It is possible to be too clear: excessive clarity can produce redundancy and frustrate students rather than help them.
The field's experimental research base on teacher clarity is described as dated and stagnating, with the authors calling for renewed, more precise study.
quotes: Instructors are well advised to continue using clarity to foster student learning. However, much of the quality experimental work is dated, and current instructional communication research on teacher clarity has been stagnating
